old: laid it on the center grip of the bow; the rest
new: laid it on the center grip of the bow, for the rest
reason: Butler: “He took an arrow that was lying upon the table—for those which the Achaeans were so shortly about to taste were all inside the quiver—he laid it …” has no semicolon, and his “for” gives the reason the arrow came from the table; the lead's reorder drops that causal link (Voice and form: cause must survive a restructure) and adds a semicolon of the kind Book 7 M-6 turned into periods. “, for” restores Butler's word, removes the added mark, and keeps the action in one unbroken movement.

old: though Iphitus was his guest. He feared neither heaven’s vengeance nor respected
new: though Iphitus was his guest, for Heracles neither feared heaven’s vengeance nor respected
reason: Butler: “though he was his guest, for he feared not heaven’s vengeance, nor yet respected his own table”. Now that the accepted edit names Iphitus, the next sentence's bare “He” first points back to Iphitus. The draft's “feared neither … nor respected” is also faulty parallelism, and it had dropped Butler's “for”. Naming Heracles and restoring “for” fixes all three.
